title: Metallic bonding
learningObjective: Know how to represent a metallic lattice by a 2D diagram; Understand metallic bonding in terms of electrostatic attractions; Explain typical physical properties of metals, including electrical conductivity and malleability

sections.title: Metallic bonding — the chapter map
sections.markdown:
Chapter 7 (u1:c07) explained compounds built by electron **transfer** — metals
handing electrons to non-metals to make ionic lattices. Chapter 8 (u1:c08)
explained compounds built by electron **sharing** — non-metals holding each
other with covalent bonds. This chapter answers a different question entirely:
what holds a **metal** together? A metal is an element on its own. There is no
non-metal to hand electrons to and nothing to share with — yet copper keeps its
shape, steel frames carry whole buildings, and aluminium survives being beaten
into foil. The bonding inside a metal is the third and final bonding model of
the course, and it reuses ideas you already own: ion formation from Chapter 7
plus electrons that are free to move.

All three objectives of record for this lesson are **chemistry-only**
specification statements — assessed in **Paper 2 (2C) only**; they do not
appear on Paper 1 (1C) and they are **not** shared with Science Double Award:

- know how to represent a metallic lattice by a **2D diagram** (spec 1.52C);
- understand metallic bonding in terms of **electrostatic attractions**
  (spec 1.53C);
- explain typical **physical properties of metals**, including electrical
  conductivity and malleability (spec 1.54C).

The lesson runs in three movements after this map: the model itself — how
sodium atoms become a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised
electrons, and exactly how you draw it; what the model predicts about melting
points, by climbing the sodium-to-magnesium comparison; and the two properties
examiners love — conductivity and malleability — ending with the close that
ties every property back to the one structure sentence. Work through the
sections in order; each one's model feeds the next one's explanations.

:::prior-knowledge
Four pieces of earlier work carry this lesson. **Electronic configurations**
from Chapter 3 (u1:c03) — sodium is [2, 8, 1] and magnesium is [2, 8, 2], and
you should read those strings instantly, because the number of outer electrons
runs the whole chapter. **Groups** from Chapter 4 (u1:c04) — the group number
tells you the outer-electron count and the ion charge: Group 1 gives 1+ ions,
Group 2 gives 2+. **Ionic bonding** from Chapter 7 (u1:c07) — the words
"lattice" and "ion" are already yours, along with the rule that ionic
substances conduct only when molten or dissolved because then their ions are
free to move. **Covalent bonding** from Chapter 8 (u1:c08) — the contrast
model: metals share nothing; their outer electrons are released to roam.
:::

:::exam-hint
Everything in this lesson is chemistry-only: Paper 2C territory, never Paper
1C, and Double Award candidates can set the chapter aside. The questions are
short and extremely predictable — draw a labelled 2-D metallic lattice; define
metallic bonding in terms of electrostatic attraction; then a chain of
"explain why" parts: why magnesium's melting point beats sodium's, why the
metal conducts when solid, why it can be hammered into new shapes. Learn the
three explanations as three stories with fixed opening lines and the marks
follow mechanically.
:::

:::misconception
"A metal is just a pile of metal atoms touching each other." No — the atoms do
not survive intact inside a metal. Each atom's outer electron is released into
a shared pool, so what the lattice actually contains is **positive ions**, not
atoms, with the released electrons moving between them. Learners who picture
neutral atoms in a pile cannot explain conduction or ion charges. Learners who
picture ions plus a mobile electron sea can answer every question this chapter
can ask.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.52C, 1.53C and 1.54C items — the chemistry-only
route badge, the three-objective map, and the contrast with the transfer and
sharing models of Chapters 7 and 8. If you can say in one sentence why neither
ionic bonding nor covalent bonding can hold a piece of copper together, you
are ready for the model itself.
:::

sections.title: Metallic bonding — positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons
sections.markdown:
Watch sodium build a metal, because one atom tells the whole story. A sodium
atom has the electronic configuration [2, 8, 1] — a single outer electron. When
sodium atoms bond together to form the solid metal, that outer electron
**leaves its atom** and becomes free to move throughout the whole structure.
The electron is said to be **[[delocalised-electron]]**: no longer attached to
any particular atom or pair of atoms — picture it flowing around through the
entire metal. The atom it left behind is no longer neutral: 11 protons now
pull on only 10 electrons, so a sodium ion, Na⁺, remains.

Multiply that event by the enormous number of atoms in even the smallest piece
of metal and you reach the structure sentence of the whole chapter: **a
metallic structure consists of a [[lattice]] — a regular arrangement — of
positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons**. The bonding holding it
together, **[[metallic-bonding]]**, is the **electrostatic forces of
attraction between each positive ion and the delocalised electrons**. Every
ion pulls on the electrons around it; the electrons pull back on every ion;
and that two-way attraction — the same electrostatic idea that held ionic
lattices and covalent molecules together — locks the whole metal into shape.

Spec 1.52C asks you to put this structure on paper in two dimensions. Draw a
grid of Na⁺ symbols in neat rows and columns, then scatter dots or small
circles in the gaps between them for the delocalised electrons, and label one
of each: "Na⁺ ion" at a grid point, "delocalised electron" in a gap. The
feature the mark scheme insists on is **regularity** — the ions must sit in a
regular repeating arrangement, not a random scatter. Different metals arrange
their ions in slightly different patterns, but nobody expects you to reproduce
a real crystal: a tidy grid is always accepted.

Two structural facts complete the model. First, a metal is a **giant
structure**: there are no individual molecules anywhere in it, and every
positive ion in the lattice attracts **all** the delocalised electrons — not
just its nearest neighbours. Second, the charge on each ion is fixed by the
atom's outer-shell count: every Group 1 metal forms 1+ ions and every Group 2
metal forms 2+ ions. Hold on to that charge rule — it becomes the engine of
the melting-point story in the next section.

:::key-point
Keep the conduction rules of the two structure types separate, because
questions live on the contrast. **Ionic compounds** conduct when **molten or
in aqueous solution**, because their ions are free to move; they do **not**
conduct when solid, because the ions are locked in place in the lattice.
**Metals** conduct when **solid or molten**, because the delocalised electrons
are free to move. The moving particle is different in each case — ions there,
electrons here — and mixing up the two is the single most expensive error in
this topic.
:::

:::exam-hint
Diagram marks are mechanical. Score them by checking four things: (1) the ions
are drawn in a **regular arrangement**; (2) the ion symbols carry their
**charges** — Na⁺, Mg²⁺; (3) electrons appear **between** the ions, not
inside them; (4) the electrons are labelled "delocalised electrons". For the
definition part of the question, both halves must appear: the force
(**electrostatic attraction**) **and** the two players it acts between
(**positive ions** and **delocalised electrons**). One half without the other
drops the mark.
:::

:::exam-hint
When you write symbol equations, a metal is always written as the plain atom
symbol — Na, Mg, Cu — never as an ion: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. The structure as a
whole carries no charge: thinking about the metal as a whole, the number of
delocalised electrons exactly balances the number of positive charges on the
ions. Learners who have just met metallic bonding sometimes start decorating
metal symbols with + signs; the ion charges belong inside the structure
diagram, not in the equation.
:::

:::misconception
"The sea of delocalised electrons makes the metal negative — or the ions make it positive."
Neither: the metal is **neutral**. Count the charges in sodium: every Na⁺
contributes exactly +1, and every atom's released electron contributes exactly
−1 to the pool. Each positive charge is balanced by a negative one, so the
piece of metal carries no charge overall. The charges only divide the labour —
ions hold the lattice points, electrons roam between them — they never sum to
anything but zero.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.52C and 1.53C items — drawing the labelled 2-D
lattice and defining metallic bonding as the electrostatic attraction between
the positive ions and the delocalised electrons. Drill the definition as one
sentence until it is automatic, then draw the sodium lattice from memory:
regular grid, charged ions, labelled electrons in the gaps.
:::

sections.title: Physical properties of metals
sections.markdown:
Most metals are hard, with high melting points — and the model explains both
facts in a single move. The electrostatic forces of attraction between the
positive ions and the delocalised electrons are **strong**. Pulling the
structure apart means fighting that attraction everywhere at once, so it takes
an enormous amount of energy, and the metal stays solid until it is heated
strongly. Whenever an exam asks you to justify hardness or a high melting
point, the answer is that attraction, and the energy needed to overcome it.

The comparison of sodium with magnesium turns the model into a prediction
machine. Both atoms release their outer electrons into the shared pool, but
they do not release the same number. Sodium atoms have one outer electron
each, so sodium's lattice is held together by 1+ ions and one delocalised
electron per atom — the bonding, as metals go, is quite weak, which is why
sodium is fairly soft with a low melting point for a metal. Magnesium atoms
have two outer electrons, both of which are delocalised, leaving ions that
carry a 2+ charge — and there is a much stronger electrostatic attraction
between the 2+ ions and the denser sea of delocalised electrons. Stronger
attraction means
more energy needed to break it, so magnesium's melting point sits well above
sodium's.

| Metal | Outer electrons released per atom | Ion charge | Attraction to the electron sea | Melting point |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sodium | 1 | 1+ | weaker | lower — soft for a metal |
| Magnesium | 2 | 2+ | much stronger | higher |

Attach a piece of metal to a power source and the delocalised electrons move
**through the metal**. Electrons are attracted towards the positive terminal
of the source and flow away along the wire; electrons flow in from the
negative terminal to replace them. A steady stream of electrons passes through
the lattice — and because the electrons were already free to move everywhere
in the structure, the metal conducts in the **solid** state, with no melting
required. Nothing in the lattice itself needs to move for a metal to carry a
current.

:::maths-skills
Read the sodium–magnesium comparison as a chain of linked quantities, not four
separate facts: **outer electrons released → ion charge → strength of
attraction → melting point**. Change one link (1 becomes 2) and every later
link steps up with it. Data questions hand you melting points or boiling
points for three consecutive metals and expect exactly this chain as the
explanation — quote the links in order, ending at the property the question
names.
:::

:::key-point
The one-line law of the whole section: **stronger attraction between the ions
and the delocalised electrons means a higher melting point**. Sodium's single
outer electron buys it a 1+ ion and weak bonding — soft, low melting point for
a metal. Magnesium's two buy a 2+ ion and much stronger bonding. When an exam
asks you to explain a melting-point difference between metals, that law plus
the charge arithmetic is the complete answer.
:::

:::exam-hint
Conduction answers have a fixed three-step shape: name the mobile particle
(**the delocalised electrons**), state that they are **free to move** through
the structure, and finish with **carry charge** through the metal. If the
question contrasts structure types, add the ionic side: ionic substances
conduct only when molten or dissolved, because then it is the **ions** that
move. "Ions move" written about a solid metal, and "electrons move" written
about a solid ionic compound, are the two answers that cost the mark.
:::

:::misconception
"Metals conduct because their ions can move through the metal." In a **solid**
metal the ions cannot move at all — they are locked at their lattice points,
which is exactly why the metal keeps its shape. The only mobile charge
carriers are the delocalised electrons. In a **molten ionic compound** the
ions really do move and conduct — but that is the ionic story from Chapter 7
(u1:c07), and it must not be pasted onto metals.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.54C items — explaining electrical conductivity and
the melting-point ladder in terms of ionic charges and the delocalised
electrons. Rehearse the two chains aloud: electrons-move-so-it-conducts-when-
solid, and more-outer-electrons → higher-charge → stronger-attraction →
higher-melting-point.
:::

sections.title: Metals are malleable — and ductile
sections.markdown:
A metal is **[[malleable]]**: hammer it and it flattens into a new shape
instead of shattering. The model explains this with a single motion. Applying
a force makes the **layers of positive ions slide over each other** — and
nothing about the bonding breaks when they do. After the slide, every ion is
still surrounded by the same sea of delocalised electrons attracting it exactly
as before, because every ion attracts **all** the electrons, wherever the ions
end up. The structure rearranges; the attraction never switches off.

Set that beside the ionic crystals of Chapter 7 (u1:c07) and the difference
becomes unforgettable. Slide a layer of an ionic crystal and like charges are
dragged face to face — attraction flips to repulsion, and the crystal shatters,
which is why ionic crystals are brittle. In a metal no such disaster is
possible: the electron sea surrounds every ion in its new position just as it
did in the old one, so the layers glide and the lattice re-seals itself. Same
lattice idea, same electrostatic attraction — but the mobile electrons make
one material bend and the other break.

Metals are also **[[ductile]]**: they can be drawn out into wires. The
explanation is the same sliding-layers story told lengthways. Pull the metal
and its layers slip past each other while the [[delocalised-electron]]s keep
every ion bonded to its surroundings, so the wire stretches and thins instead
of snapping. Copper's job inside a cable uses the pair of properties at once:
ductile enough to be drawn into fine wire, conductive enough to carry the
current through it.

This chapter completes the bonding picture of Unit 1. **Transfer** builds
ionic lattices; **sharing** builds covalent molecules and giant covalent
structures; **release** builds metallic lattices. Three ways of arranging
electrostatic attraction, three families of structure, three sets of
properties. Every structure-and-bonding question from here to the end of the
course is one of those three stories — or, in the best questions, a comparison
that asks you to tell them apart.

:::summary
- A metal is a **giant lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised
  electrons**: each atom releases its outer electron to a pool that moves
  freely through the whole structure.
- **Metallic bonding** is the electrostatic attraction between those positive
  ions and the delocalised electrons — the force that holds the lattice
  together.
- Ion charges follow the group — Group 1 metals form 1+ ions, Group 2 metals
  form 2+ — so releasing more outer electrons means a higher ion charge,
  stronger attraction and a **higher melting point**: magnesium above sodium.
- Metals **conduct when solid or molten** because the delocalised electrons
  are free to move; the ionic contrast is ions moving only when molten or
  dissolved.
- Metals are **malleable and ductile** because layers of ions slide over each
  other without breaking the bonding — the property ionic crystals lack.
:::

:::can-you
- draw a labelled 2-D diagram of a metallic lattice — regular rows of charged
  ions with delocalised electrons between them (spec 1.52C)?
- define metallic bonding in one sentence that names the force and both
  players (spec 1.53C)?
- explain, link by link, why magnesium's melting point is higher than
  sodium's (spec 1.54C)?
- explain why a metal conducts when solid while a solid ionic compound does
  not?
- explain malleability and ductility with the sliding-layers argument — and
  say why ionic crystals cannot do the same?
If every answer comes without looking back, the chapter is banked — move on to
electrolysis (u1:c10), where charges on the move meet their master application.
:::

:::exam-hint
Malleability answers are two sentences, always: **"the layers of positive ions
slide over each other"** and **"the bonding is not affected — the ions are
still attracted to the delocalised electrons."** If the question asks why
metals differ from ionic crystals, add the third sentence: sliding an ionic
layer brings like charges together and the crystal shatters, while in a metal
the electron sea keeps every ion bonded wherever it moves. "Layers slide" on
its own earns the first mark and stops — the intact-bonding sentence is where
the second one lives.
:::

:::misconception
"Bending a metal breaks its bonds and re-forms them." No — the bonding never
breaks, and that is precisely why the metal survives. As the layers slide, the
delocalised electrons re-arrange around the moving ions instantly, so the
attraction between ions and electrons is continuous throughout. If the bonds
actually broke, the metal would crack like an ionic crystal. The phrase to
avoid in answers is "bonds break and re-make"; the phrase to use is "the
bonding is unaffected".
:::

:::cross-curricular
The properties you have just explained are the reason metals run the modern
world. Steel frames stand because strong metallic bonding makes steel hard.
Copper wins the wiring job because it conducts electricity and draws into
wire. Aluminium foil and car-body panels exist because the metal is malleable.
Materials engineers choose a metal exactly the way you answer the exam
question — property first, with the structure-and-bonding explanation running
underneath.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.54C items — the sliding-layers explanation for
malleability and ductility, plus the full property set of the chapter. If you
can produce every property in this chapter from the one structure sentence —
positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons — the topic is yours.
:::
